significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish the form-(iii) law that subliminal traits are “robust to random and single-unit ablation and to moderate compression—yet efficiently removable by a small targeted low-rank ablation,” with greater compression robustness than matched overt traits; this fixes a qualitative ordering among independently measurable ablation and retention curves. It establishes both a phenomenon (trait persistence under pruning and quantization) and a mechanistic constraint (low-dimensional yet parameter-distributed storage), thereby predicting responses to several model modifications beyond the original transmission behavior studied in “Subliminal Learning: Language Models Transmit Behavioral Traits via Hidden Signals in Data.” The negative branch is informative if the matched robustness predicted in the abstract occurs, because it supports the stated alternative that subliminal and explicit fine-tuning “produce the same kind of change,” although failure of only one subprediction would be less decisive; true and false outcomes are nevertheless distinguishable. In the topic-substitution check, merely restating “extend research on subliminal learning” would not justify this score: the claim-specific robustness ordering and subliminal-versus-overt comparison make it sharper than the median extension, though storage geometry is not the whole transmission mechanism.

reach.justification: The claim hands downstream users the “robustness curves and the rank/parameter budget needed to remove the trait” plus a “targeted low-rank ablation,” providing a measurable diagnostic and an intervention rather than only an explanation. These are post-acquisition handles, but the ablation can be applied before deployment, giving auditors or deployers an action window when deciding whether to quantize, prune, gate, or ship a model. After per-model re-extraction, the conclusion still predicts a transferable qualitative relation—random pruning should preserve the trait while targeted low-rank removal should suppress it—although it does not predict architecture-independent numerical ranks and the hypothesis states no explicit architecture or training-regime scope. The topic-substitution check does not preserve the score: generic subliminal-learning research supplies no such removal budget or compression rule, whereas this claim specifically supports practitioner uptake beyond researchers studying transmission.
